anubis.texto: Jackal-headed god, protector of the necropolis and patron of mummification. He performs the weighing of the dead person's heart against the feather of Maat.
anubis.thot: Solemn, yes. But you should see him try to dance at a festival. Not another word.

thot.texto: God of writing, wisdom and the moon. He is shown as an ibis, or as a man with an ibis head. He recorded the result of your weighing.
thot.thot: I wrote this entry. In all humility, it's the best one in the book.

maat.texto: Maat is the goddess and the idea of truth, order and justice. Her symbol is the ostrich feather. The opposite of Maat is Isfet, chaos.
maat.thot: A heart lighter than her feather. Sounds poetic until it's literally your life at stake.

ammit.texto: The devourer of hearts: crocodile head, lion forequarters, hippopotamus hindquarters. She devours the hearts that weigh too much at the judgment.
ammit.thot: Don't invite her to dinner. It's literally the only thing she does.

duat.texto: The Egyptian underworld that the dead travel through on their way to the final judgment.
duat.thot: Cold, dark, and with a frankly outrageous waiting line.

aaru.texto: The Field of Reeds, ruled by Osiris: the paradise of the righteous. An eternal, abundant version of the fields of Egypt, where people still farmed.
aaru.thot: Yes, even in paradise you keep plowing. The Egyptians loved their land even after death.

ba.texto: One of the parts of the Egyptian soul, depicted as a bird with a human head.
ba.thot: Your ba wanders around keeping memories even you don't remember. Handy and a little unsettling.

sheut.texto: The shadow, another of the parts that make up a person in Egyptian belief.
sheut.thot: Don't confuse your sheut with the creatures that chase you at night. Although, to be fair, the confusion is understandable.

cultivos.texto: Emmer wheat was the base of bread and beer. Flax was used for clothing and mummy bandages. Papyrus grew in the Nile marshes and gave the material for writing.
cultivos.thot: Three plants, a whole civilization on top. Not bad for mere green stalks.

amuletos.texto: The ankh is the symbol of life. The heart scarab was placed on the mummy's chest so the heart would not speak against the deceased during the judgment.
amuletos.thot: An amulet that covers your own heart's mouth. The Egyptians thought of everything.

kemet.texto: "The black land": that's what the Egyptians called their country, for the fertile silt the Nile left behind. There were three seasons: Akhet (flood), Peret (sowing and growth) and Shemu (harvest).
kemet.thot: We're in Peret. Sowing. It's literally what the name says.

heraldo.texto: A creature from THIS story, not from Egyptian texts: no papyrus mentions a herald of Ammit. It has her features (crocodile, lion, hippo) because it serves her.
heraldo.thot: I'm filing this as fiction. My reputation as a scribe won't be stained by an invented monster.

shabti.texto: Small figures buried with the dead. Their job: doing the farm work for them in the afterlife, so they could rest.
shabti.thot: An army of little dolls working for free for all eternity. Enviable.

senet.texto: One of the oldest known Egyptian board games. It was associated with the soul's journey after death.
senet.thot: Iry cheats. I saw it. I wrote it down.
